name: Ngbandi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Nelson, Quentin D. 1952. Linguistic problems in Ngbandi. The Bible Translator 3(1): 39-45.
catalog_locator: p. 41, section I.B 'Relationship to the lingua franca' (of, archive.org; page pin)
catalog_quote: The Bantu words are invariably accented on the penultimate (next to the last) syllable. There is tone in a two-register system, but for the most part it seems to be of lexical importance only, making differences in meaning between a few words, but it is not of grammatical importance. The Sudanic languages in the Ubangi, on the other hand, consist basically of monosyllabic words, that is, most of their “words” in simplest form consist of one syllable. They make very little use of affixation. In fact, the Ngbandi language, judging from my present analysis, will probably have no elements which need be considered as prefixes or suffixes. Accent or stress does not exist. The tonal system is extremely well developed, there being three registers of tone plus glides. These tones are not only lexical but also morphological (of grammatical importance) as will be seen later in this article.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngbandi has no word accent/stress; it is a tone language with three register tones (low, mid, high) plus glides, tone being both lexical and grammatical. Words are basically monosyllabic, so there is no positional stress rule to state.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Nelson. Czermak's 1926 review (Anthropos 21: 659, second-hand) reports that Lekens 1923 devotes a chapter to 'Klemtoon' (dynamic accent): a syllable can be given expiratory prominence for emphasis without changing its tone — i.e. an emphatic, not lexical, prominence.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (explicit contrast with Bantu penultimate word accent); citation forms not discussed. The source is a short missionary-linguist article, not a full phonology; the scanned reads 'words. that' and 'arammatical', corrected here to 'words, that' and 'grammatical'. Consistent with Toronzoni 1992: 416 (every vowel bears a tone; no stress mentioned) and Mortier 1948-49 (lexical tone patterns only).
new_statements.identity_note: Nelson 1952 describes 'Ngbandi (popularly called Mongbandi or Mongwandi)' of the Ubangi district of the Belgian Congo, with the main population in the east of the region (Mobayi/Yakoma/Uele side) — the variety Glottolog files under nort2774 (same assignment as Lekens and Toronzoni); the article does not name a dialect. Southern Ngbandi [nbw] (Budjala/Ngiri area) is a separate Glottolog languoid and is not distinguished by Nelson. Lekens 1923 (per Czermak) treats mainly the eastern dialect; Toronzoni 1989/1992 the Ngbandi of north-west Zaïre.

new_statements.quote: 16 — Benevens den eigenaardigen muzikalen toon eigen aan elke lettergreep, geeft men soms aan zekere lettergrepen of woorden ook nog een klemtoon om meer nadruk op die woorden te geven. Die klemtoon is dan niet, zooals in onze Europeesche talen, van chromatischen maar louter van expiratorischen en quantitatieven aard, t. t. z. dat de nadruk op een woord of lettergreep gelegd, niets verandert aan de toonhoogte, maar eenvoudig bestaat in een met meer kracht uitgesproken en langer gerokken geluid. B. v.: Kódoro, légè, ngbî. In deze voorbeelden zijn de eerste lettergrepen langer en sterker, als men op die woorden wil steunen.
new_statements.translation: 16 — Besides the peculiar musical tone proper to every syllable, one sometimes also gives certain syllables or words a stress (klemtoon) in order to put more emphasis on those words. That stress is then not, as in our European languages, of a chromatic [pitch] nature but purely expiratory and quantitative, i.e. the emphasis laid on a word or syllable changes nothing in the pitch, but simply consists of a sound pronounced with more force and drawn out longer. E.g.: Kódoro, légè, ngbî. In these examples the first syllables are longer and stronger, when one wants to lean on [emphasise] those words. [p. 9 continues: 'Although le of légè, ngbî, and ko of kodoro are long, they still each keep their own tone'; p. 10: even sentence-finally a word keeps its own tone. p. 1 art. 2: 'The vowels are as a rule short ... Long vowels do not really occur. Only when one wants to lean on a word is the vowel held longer; e.g. lege, kodoro, ngbî.']

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (world-r2) has an empty rule; the existing statement (Nelson 1952: 'Accent or stress does not exist', tone language) reads 'no word stress'. Lekens is compatible: he describes no lexical word stress, only tone on every syllable, and adds detail Nelson lacks: an optional emphatic 'klemtoon' (expiratory + durational, pitch-neutral) which in his examples falls on the first syllable of the emphasised word. This confirms first-hand what Czermak's 1926 review (held by the project) reported second-hand. Not a placement contradiction; at most a nuance (Nelson: no stress at all; Lekens: emphatic stress exists but is not lexical).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngbandi is described as a tone language (low, mid, high plus contour tones on every syllable; Toonleer pp. 5-10). There is no lexical or fixed word stress in the description: 'klemtoon' is an optional emphatic prominence given 'sometimes' to certain syllables or words for emphasis, realised as greater force and length with pitch unchanged; in the author's examples (kódoro, légè, ngbî) it is the word's first syllable that is lengthened and strengthened under emphasis. Vowel length is otherwise non-existent (p. 1 art. 2: long vowels occur only under such emphasis).
new_statements.exceptions: None as stress exceptions. Related remarks: p. 9-10, emphasised (lengthened) syllables keep their lexical tone; sentence-final words keep their own tone whether the sentence is a question or statement, with only a hard-to-write nuance of tone in questions (p. 10); p. 1 art. 2, vowels are short except under emphasis.
new_statements.identity_note: Lekens 1923 is based mainly on the East dialect of Ngbandi (p. xvii, Tanghe's introduction: 'deze spraakkunst, die hoofdzakelijk volgens het Oost-dialekt is opgemaakt', signed Abumombazi 1921; Abumombazi/Yakoma area), i.e. Northern Ngbandi nort2774, eastern variety; pp. xv-xviii contrast West- and Oost-Ngbandi word forms.

tone_statements.quote: Éénlettergrepige naamwoorden zijn laag-, middel-, hccg-, of dubbeltonig. Middeltonige komen het meest voor ; de dubbeltonige zijn schaars. [p. 138:] Ziehier hun procent : laagtonige ... 28 op 100 middeltonige . . 40 " 100 hoogtonige . . 29 " 100 dubbeltonige . 9 " 100 [...] [p. 140, B. Werkwoorden, 1. Éénlettergrepige:] De drie tonen zijn evenredig vertegenwoordigd. De dubbeltoon minder. Deze is altijd hoog-laag. [...] Bij de tweelettergrepige werkwoorder bestaan maar drie schakeringen van tonen: 1) laag-Iaag, H) hoog-laag, 111 ) hoog-hoog.
tone_statements.translation: Monosyllabic nouns are low-, mid-, high- or double-toned. Mid-toned ones are the most frequent; the double-toned ones are rare. Here are their percentages: low-toned 28 per 100, mid-toned 40, high-toned 29, double-toned 9. [Verbs, monosyllabic:] The three tones are equally represented. The double tone less so; it is always high-low. [...] For disyllabic verbs there are only three tone patterns: I) low-low, II) high-low, III) high-high.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.n_tones: 3 level (L, M, H) + contour ('dubbeltoon', H-L on verbs) — for Ngbandi, sister…

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict. Nelson 1952 (existing statement) says accent or stress does not exist in Ngbandi; Lekens 1923 (p. 9, art. 16) says that besides the tone on every syllable an emphatic 'klemtoon' is sometimes given to certain syllables or words, purely expiratory and quantitative with pitch unchanged, and that in his examples (kódoro, légè, ngbî) the first syllable is lengthened and strengthened under emphasis. Both agree there is no lexical/contrastive word stress and that the language is tonal; Lekens adds the emphatic (pragmatic) prominence, which Czermak 1926 had summarised as 'dynamischer Akzent'. If the catalog wants a single line: tone language, no lexical word stress; optional emphatic stress realised as initial-syllable lengthening/force per Lekens.
